The walkthroughs are executable notebooks that work through the concepts 
behind Open Road Risk's modelling pipeline. They sit between the formal 
[literature review](../literature/literature-index.qmd) — which cites and 
synthesises peer-reviewed sources — and the [project pages](../project/project-overview.qmd), 
which document what the pipeline does. Each walkthrough takes a concept 
or argument from the literature and works through it in code, with plots 
and prose.

The format is Python in Quarto, rendered as HTML on this site. Each page
also exports as a Jupyter notebook that you can download, open, and
modify. The notebooks live alongside the walkthrough sources in
[`quarto/walkthroughs`](https://github.com/ThomasHSimm/open-road-risk/tree/main/quarto/walkthroughs)
on GitHub. Data is mostly synthetic where the point is to show how a method
behaves; in some cases real STATS19 or AADF samples are used, published
as Kaggle datasets where the real distribution matters.

The walkthroughs are looser than the literature pages. They include the 
intuition, the simulations, and the moments where the argument needed a 
detour to land. Where the literature pages cite, the walkthroughs show.

## Reading order

The walkthroughs are designed to stand alone but they build on each 
other. A reader new to count modelling should start with the crash 
frequency walkthrough — it covers the distributional foundations that 
later pages assume. Readers who already know Poisson and negative 
binomial regression can skip to whichever topic is relevant.

The walkthroughs deliberately do not replicate what already exists. The 
Leeds Institute for Transport Studies' [Reproducible Road Safety Research 
with R](https://itsleeds.github.io/rrsrr/) is the canonical resource for 
STATS19 data handling, and the [stats19 R package](https://docs.ropensci.org/stats19/) 
is the de facto standard for working with the data in R. The walkthroughs 
focus on modelling rather than data handling, and use Python rather 
than R.
